Without Wi-Fi RTT, distance to the router is estimated from signal strength rather than measured directly. The heatmap still works.
Anyone in range can read any traffic that is not using HTTPS. Turn on WPA2 or WPA3 in the router settings.
Your network uses the old WPA
First-generation WPA can be broken. Switch to WPA2 or WPA3 in the router settings — every modern device supports it.
WPS is on for your network
The WPS button uses an eight-digit PIN that can be guessed within hours. Turn WPS off in the router settings; the ordinary Wi-Fi password keeps working exactly as before.
This is the strongest standard available today. Nothing needs changing.
The Wi-Fi password keeps traffic away from anyone outside the network. If the router supports WPA3, using it is better still.
Anyone can join a network like this, and the traffic inside it is readable by every other device that joins. Avoid banking or entering passwords there.
WEP has been broken since 2001 and can now be opened in minutes with free tools. In practice it is equivalent to an open network.
A WPS PIN is only eight digits and is checked in two separate halves, so it can be guessed far faster than an ordinary Wi-Fi password.
Duplicate network names with different protection

Two transmitters share a name but differ in how they are protected. This happens when an old router was never switched off, but it is also the pattern a rogue access point uses to lure devices into connecting. Make sure you recognise both.
Hiding the name adds no security — the transmitter is still visible, and devices that remember it end up broadcasting that name everywhere they go looking for it.
Old WPA uses TKIP, which has practical attacks against it. WPA2 and above are its replacement.

Wi-Fi has a shape — strong in some corners of a home, dead in others, and invisible everywhere.
This app measures its strength as you walk, tracks your position with ARCore, then paints it as a 3D plan complete with the weakest spot and a suggestion for where the router should move.

Your surveys, room plans, Wi-Fi readings and landmark photos are saved in app storage. Location permission enables Wi-Fi scanning and can attach a location to your survey; the camera supports AR tracking and optional photos. Google AdMob processes advertising and diagnostic data according to your privacy choices. Google Play processes purchases. Speed tests contact Cloudflare, and network tests contact the selected hosts. Sharing a report or image sends its contents to the destination you choose. Read the privacy policy for details.

Strong in some corners of the house, dead in others, and you cannot see any of it.
This app measures its strength as you walk, then paints it as a 3D plan — complete with the strongest point, the dead spots, and a suggestion for where the router should move.

Location — Android requires it to read Wi-Fi network names and to scan for nearby networks. Not our choice; without it the system refuses to hand over the data.
Camera — used to track your position in the room so every measurement has a coordinate, and to photograph landmarks.
All of it is processed on this phone. Nothing is sent anywhere.

A 3D plan of the home with a signal heatmap — both the colour and the height of each tile mean signal strength.
A green pillar marks the strongest point, red the weakest, purple the suggested router position. The white ribbon is the route you walked.
Press the camera button while scanning to mark a place — a desk, the kitchen, a bedroom — then name it afterwards.
The result can be exported as an image or a written report.

**Walk slowly**, at the pace of an unhurried stroll. Fast movement makes tracking lose its place.
**Hold the phone at chest height**, camera facing forward and slightly down.
**Point at a wall now and then** for 2–3 seconds, especially one with a pattern — a cupboard, a poster, a door frame. That is what makes the room shape real rather than an estimated box.
**Cover every room**, including the corners with bad signal. Those are exactly what this is looking for.

Tile height = signal strength. The white ribbon is the route you walked, and the purple needle points north.
Tile colour means signal strength, and so does its height. Red is weak, green is strong.
Drag to rotate, pinch to zoom. Tap a blue pillar for the photo.

ICMP echo is tried first, which is the round trip a network engineer means. Some hosts and mobile networks drop it, and a TCP connection stands in — that figure includes the handshake, so it reads a little higher.
Distance is inferred from signal strength with generic constants, not measured. A wall alone can double it.
Android asks you to confirm before saving it. The phone then connects for real, not just inside this app.
This one needs a password, so it is joined in the system Wi-Fi picker. An app is not allowed to connect a phone on its own.
You are connected to this network
Tap a network for full detail
Networks on your exact channel take turns with you — the link stays clean but shares the airtime, so everything slows down together.
Networks that only overlap never coordinate with you. That shows up as retries and jitter rather than lower speed, and it is the worse of the two even when the number is smaller.
Nothing else is on or near your channel right now.
Nothing on this band to rank.
5 GHz is the emptier band here. It carries less far and is stopped by walls more easily, but where it reaches it will be the faster of the two.
2.4 GHz is the emptier band here, which is unusual. It also reaches further, so on this spot it is the better choice.
Only one band is in use around here.
Graded on what each beacon advertises. That says nothing about how strong the password is, how old the firmware is, or who already has the key.
No wall found yet. Stop about 1.5 m from one, keep the camera on it, and step slowly left and right for a few seconds — that sideways movement is what lets a wall be measured.
This connection is using everything both sides support.
You are on the slower band

The same network is also broadcasting on 5 GHz at %1$d dBm, while you are on 2.4 GHz at %2$d dBm. Phones often join the slower band once from far away and never move back. Forgetting and rejoining the network usually fixes it.

The link is using %1$d MHz. On 5 GHz a router will normally offer 80 MHz, which carries roughly four times as much. The setting is in the router\'s own panel, usually called channel width or bandwidth.
Your phone is newer than your router
This phone speaks %1$s; the router is offering %2$s. Nothing is broken — it simply means a newer router would be faster for you, and an older one would not.
This phone supports WPA3, the current standard. Switching the router to WPA2/WPA3 mixed mode costs nothing and protects this connection better.
Link running well below its ceiling
Negotiated at %1$d Mbps against a ceiling of %2$d Mbps. Distance, a busy channel and interference all cause this — the 3D map is what tells them apart.
No scan has recorded neighbouring transmitters yet. Run a 3D scan and this fills in from the same walk.
Left at %1$d dBm, joined at %2$d dBm
Held on too long. A stronger radio was already available well before the phone moved — this is what makes a room feel dead even with a node in it.
Several transmitters were in range but the phone never switched between them during this walk. That is normal on a short scan.
Android lets an app ask for a fresh scan four times per two minutes, so each transmitter is caught at a handful of places along the walk rather than continuously.
Runs a short download every few seconds while you walk, so the map can show what each room can actually carry — not just how loud the radio is there. Costs a few megabytes of data.

Signal strength and speed are not the same thing. A strong reading on a channel three neighbours are sharing can carry less than a weaker one on an empty channel — which is why moving a router on the strength of a dBm map alone so often disappoints.

AR scanning uses Google Play Services for AR (ARCore), provided by Google. Google processes service data under its Privacy Policy. Tap to read.
Channels are rated by how many neighbours share them and how loud those neighbours are. Wide carriers count against every channel they span — an 80 MHz hog is a problem for four channels, not one.

Score 0–10: empty channels earn 10, and each overlapping network or loud rival pulls it down. DFS channels are legal to use but must be vacated if radar is detected.

802.11mc measures actual round-trip time to an access point — distance in metres, not a signal-strength estimate. Tap a spot on the sketch where you are standing and it triangulates where the router sits.
This phone does not support Wi-Fi RTT (802.11mc), so distances can only be estimated from signal strength elsewhere in the app.

A model, not a measurement: direct path + a few dB per wall. Real coverage depends on wall material and furniture the scan cannot see.
Every abbreviation the app uses, in one line.
Decibel-milliwatts — how strong the signal is. −40 is excellent, −70 usable, −90 nearly dead.
Received Signal Strength Indicator — the dBm reading’s technical name.
The app’s name for dBm ranges, from Excellent down to Dead.
Signal strength drawn over your floor plan after an AR walk.
Switching between router nodes as you walk. Done late, it shows as a dip.
A network’s name — the thing you tap to join.
A transmitter’s hardware address. One SSID can be many BSSIDs in a mesh.
Which slice of spectrum the network uses: 2.4, 5 or 6 GHz.
A numbered lane inside a band. Sharing one is what makes Wi-Fi feel crowded.
Channels shared with radar — allowed to use, but the router may have to leave them suddenly.
How much spectrum a carrier occupies, 20 to 160 MHz. Wider is faster, overlaps more.
Other transmitters on or near your channel, competing for airtime.
Generations of the 802.11 standard (n / ac / ax / be). Newer is faster.
Round-trip time in milliseconds — how long an answer takes, not how wide the pipe is.
How much latency varies. Calls and games care about it more than raw speed.
How much data actually moves per second, in Mbps.
Extra delay a router adds under load when its buffers are too big — the classic cause of lag while downloading.
Megabits per second. Divide by 8 for megabytes.
Round-Trip Time — the Wi-Fi ranging standard that measures metres to the router.
A device’s number on the local network, like 192.168.1.5.
Your router’s own address — the door out to the internet.
The router handing out addresses automatically when devices join.
Translates names like example.com into addresses. Changing it can speed up browsing.
How phones, printers and TVs announce themselves on the local network.
How smart devices advertise what they are — TVs, speakers, cameras.
Several router nodes covering one home under one name; the phone roams between them.
